paras: The whipping of Henry at Haynesville, Louisiana, took place on a Saturday night in mid-July 1881, when a man identified as young Mr. Smith whipped a Black boy named Henry, aged 15 or 16, and ordered him to leave. The only known account, a warning notice in an Arkansas weekly, accused Henry of entering Mrs. Smith's bedroom and urged readers to "look out for him."

According to Haynesville postmaster Jas R. Smith, Henry "last Saturday night went to the bed of young Mr. Smith's wife, caught her by the feet and awoke her." Mrs. Smith called her husband, and Henry took refuge under the house. He was caught there, whipped and "given orders to leave by the enraged husband."

Henry was last seen near Mt. Pisgah church, traveling in the direction of Atlanta. His uncle came to Haynesville looking for him the following Tuesday and was reported to have said that this was not the first time Henry had been "guilty of such conduct." No report of an arrest, a charge against either party, or of what became of Henry appears in the coverage.

The Columbia Banner of Magnolia, Arkansas, printed the story on July 21, 1881, under the headline "LOOK OUT.", crediting the Haynesville postmaster as its source. The item gave only the Smith household's version, named Henry alone by race, called him "the culprit" and ended with the warning "Look out for him," treating the accusation as established. Henry's own account does not appear, and no report of the incident was found in the parish paper or in any other newspaper.
